newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Coffee holds gains, gold pauses for breath.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Coffee holds gains, gold pauses for breath.

text.p: World coffee prices held onto recent gains on Thursday as news of a strike by Colombian truck drivers and continuing prospects of a national strike in Brazil's key ports combined to intensify near-term supply concerns.
Elsewhere, commodity markets saw wheat firm slightly, while oil continued to look soft but off the day's lows. Gold remained steady after heavy selling earlier in the week.

A strike by truck drivers in Colombia, the world's second largest coffee producer, was expected to begin at midnight on Saturday, while stevedores were still to go ahead with a 48-hour national strike in Brazil's two key coffee ports after Santos.

The strike in Brazil, the world's number one coffee producer, was due to start at 1000 GMT on Friday, should negotiations fail on Thursday, in sympathy with stevedores in Santos who have been on an indefinite strike since Tuesday.
"There are two strikes coming up, the certified stocks are low and the May spread is widening," said one European trader. "A few roasters are not covered and I think May could continue to rise."
Robusta coffee futures for May were trading unchanged at $1,615 per tonne in London's Thursday afternoon, having touched an intra-day high of $1,635.
In the grain markets Chicago Board of Trade wheat looked firmer after U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) weekly export sales figures came in above expectations.
USDA data showed wheat export sales for the week ended April 10 totalled 263,900 tonnes versus expectations for 100,000 to 200,000 tonnes.
But gains were reined in by varying crop damage estimates after a weekend freeze in Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas which boosted wheat prices at the beginning of the week.
Crude oil prices for benchmark North Sea Brent Blend bounced off an intra-day low of $17.66 a barrel in London's Thursday afternoon but continued to look soft.
The June Brent futures contract hovered below $18 a a barrel as bearish sentiment persisted after recently reported rising U.S. stocks and weak gasoline demand.

Gold staunched the flow of the week's heavy losses pushing back up above $340 an ounce to touch a high of $343.30, but dealers said they saw this as a period of consolidation before a further possible downturn.
"We are probably stuck in a $340-$345 range. Rallies above $345 are increasingly likely to be sold," said Ted Arnold, precious metals analyst at Merrill Lynch in London.
Cocoa futures were slightly stronger in London's Thursday afternoon, but remained rangebound for most of the day.
Meanwhile copper and aluminium were virtually unchanged in London's afternoon, floating within a range in lackustre trading for most of the day.
"There's no impetus, no direction. It's dismal," said one floor trader, referring to the copper market.
